title: Why BEAD projects stall and how to navigate the re-bid round
summary: States are reopening BEAD bidding, sometimes for projects that have fallen through. Applicants that plan beyond the award and for the full life of the network will be better placed to compete and deliver.
body_markdown:
Virginia’s Office of Broadband has opened a re-bidding process for four defaulted Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment (BEAD) projects covering 9,799 locations,[Broadband Communities](https://bbcmag.com/virginia-reopens-bidding-on-defaulted-bead-projects/) reports. The process can run for up to three rounds, with unawarded projects and locations remaining eligible for the next. Once they are awarded, however, they leave the pool.


Virginia isn’t alone. In September, the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) issued a memo making leftover BEAD funding available for new bidding for unserved locations. NTIA has described the total “savings” as about $21 billion, to run new bidding for unserved locations, according to[Light Reading](https://www.lightreading.com/broadband/bead-non-deployment-funds-to-be-used-for-deployment-ntia) . States must review their eligible-location lists and conduct a challenge process before moving into a 90-day subgrantee selection round.


Meanwhile, awards keep moving: Georgia signed[a second BEAD agreement with AT&T](https://gta.georgia.gov/news/2026-11-17/gta-announces-second-bead-grant-agreement-att-expand-broadband-access) on November 17 covering 23,511 locations and about 6,794 miles of fiber across 26 counties. In Michigan, rural ISP consortium Helexon[signed subgrants](https://bbcmag.com/helexon-signs-bead-subgrant-agreements-in-michigan/) for more than 50,000 locations in 60 counties.


With major builds already competing for crews and equipment, applicants pursuing these new opportunities will face an even sharper question: Can they deliver what they bid for, and will the network remain competitive through future upgrade cycles?


**Why projects stall after the award**


A BEAD award is a commitment to deliver a defined service to defined locations by a defined date. As that commitment meets the realities of deployment, several pressures can put it at risk:


- **Cost assumptions break** . Make-ready work, permitting and labor costs in rural areas can exceed early estimates, putting further pressure on margins in high-cost areas.
- **Supply and staffing get tight** . Multiple projects may compete for the same contractors, splicing crews and equipment during the same build season.
- **Operations are underplanned** . Winning applicants have to connect, provision and support thousands of new subscribers, often with small teams.


None of these risks can be solved by technology alone. But network design choices can determine how much risk an operator carries for years after the ribbon-cutting.


**Design the network for its second decade**
The outside plant is the expensive, long-lived part of a fiber network. Once the fiber, splitters and drops are deployed, the main opportunity to increase capacity comes from upgrading the electronics at either end.


That makes a passive optical network (PON) roadmap an important part of long-term planning. Today’s GPON and XGS-PON can share a fiber with 50G PON, defined in the ITU-T G.9804 series. Each generation uses its own wavelengths, so an operator can add faster services on the same optical distribution network (ODN) without rebuilding it or moving existing subscribers. Our[50G PON overview](https://www.adtran.com/en/products-and-services/technology/what-is-50g-pon?utm_source=technically-speaking&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=261125-why-bead-projects-stall-and-how-to-navigate-the-re-bid-round) describes Combo PON optics that support GPON, XGS-PON and 50G PON from one optical line terminal (OLT) port.


For a BEAD applicant, that means future upgrades can focus on the electronics rather than rebuilding the outside plant. It’s a stronger story for a state reviewer weighing long-term value, and it helps protect the operator’s capital investment.


> Network design choices can determine how much risk an operator carries for years after the ribbon-cutting.


**Make operations part of the bid**


The challenge doesn’t end when the network is built. Applicants also need to show how they will connect, provision and support potentially thousands of new subscribers, without putting unsustainable pressure on their operational teams. They can strengthen their bids by showing:


- **Automated provisioning and activation** , so new subscribers can be turned up without manual configuration at each step.
- **Proactive monitoring** , so faults can be identified before they lead to a truck roll or support call.
- **Clear upgrade paths for access and aggregation** , so capacity can grow without requiring a future rebuild.


**What to do before the next round opens**


Re-bid windows will be short. Operators that want to compete should have their technology plan, supply commitments and operating model ready before bidding begins. Three questions are worth answering now:


1. Can our access platform add higher-speed PON on the same fiber, and has that been demonstrated in live networks?
2. Do our equipment lead times and staffing plans align with the bidding timetable and the build season that follows?
3. Can we show a state reviewer that we can operate the network, not just build it?


Operators with strong answers to these questions will be better placed to compete for BEAD awards, deliver on their commitments and keep their networks competitive through future upgrade cycles.

**Frequently asked questions**


**What is a BEAD re-bid round?**


A BEAD re-bid round gives states another opportunity to award funding for locations that remain unserved. This can include locations affected by defaulted projects or made eligible through additional deployment funding under NTIA guidance.


**How long do states have to run a BEAD re-bid?**


Under NTIA’s September 2026 guidance, states must first review their eligible-location lists and conduct a challenge process. They then have 90 days to conduct the new subgrantee selection round, according to[Light Reading](https://www.lightreading.com/broadband/bead-non-deployment-funds-to-be-used-for-deployment-ntia) .


**What can put a BEAD project at risk after the award?**


Cost pressures from make-ready work, permitting and labor, competition for contractors, crews and equipment, and the operational demands of connecting and supporting new subscribers can all put delivery plans under pressure.


**Can GPON, XGS-PON and 50G PON share the same fiber?**


Yes. Each PON generation uses its own wavelengths, allowing GPON, XGS-PON and 50G PON to coexist on the same optical distribution network (ODN). Combo PON optics can support all three from one optical line terminal (OLT) port.
